stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Oduya and colleagues' conclusion?
stimulus: Beetroot juice is rich in nitrate, which the body cannot use directly. Bacteria on the back of the tongue convert nitrate to nitrite, which is then absorbed into the blood and turned into nitric oxide, a compound that relaxes blood vessels. Nutrition scientist Hana Oduya and colleagues found that adults who drank beetroot juice daily for four weeks had lower resting blood pressure than adults who drank a nitrate-free juice. The researchers concluded that this drop depends on the tongue bacteria's conversion step.
choices: Beetroot juice failed to lower blood pressure in participants whose tongue bacteria had been killed by mouthwash.
Beetroot juice lowered blood pressure just as much in participants whose tongue bacteria had been killed by mouthwash.
Spinach, which also contains nitrate, lowered blood pressure less than beetroot juice did in a separate trial.
A few participants who drank beetroot juice daily showed no measurable change in their resting blood pressure.
explanation: The conclusion says the drop in blood pressure depends on the bacteria's conversion step. For that to be true, removing the bacteria should remove the effect. If the juice works just as well after the bacteria have been killed, then the conversion step isn't needed, and the conclusion is weakened directly.

A.why: You answered the opposite question. If the effect disappears when the bacteria are gone, that shows the conversion step matters, so this choice supports the conclusion.

C.why: You picked a choice about the same nutrient that doesn't test the claim. Comparing spinach with beetroot says nothing about whether the tongue bacteria are needed.

D.why: You treated a few individual exceptions as if they undercut a group result. People vary, and a handful of non-responders doesn't tell you anything about whether the bacterial step is the mechanism.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Velez's conclusion?
stimulus: In a Wisconsin forest, a woodland lily has been declining since 1990, and soil acidification has been documented throughout the region over the same period. Ecologist Marta Velez fenced twelve plots to keep out white-tailed deer and left twelve similar plots unfenced. After six years, lily density had risen in the fenced plots but not in the unfenced ones. Velez concluded that deer browsing, rather than soil acidification, is the main cause of the lily's decline.
choices: Lilies in the unfenced plots showed bite marks on most stems, while lilies in fenced plots showed almost none.
Soil acidity throughout the region rose steadily between 1990 and the start of the study.
Lily density in the fenced plots showed no change at all over the six years of the study.
The fenced plots had been placed on ground that was much less acidic than the ground under the unfenced plots.
explanation: Velez's conclusion depends on the two sets of plots being alike in everything except the fencing. If the fenced plots also had much less acidic soil, then lower acidity could explain the lilies' recovery just as well as keeping the deer out. That undermines her ruling-out of acidification.

A.why: You picked the choice that strengthens the conclusion. Bite marks only in the unfenced plots confirm that deer were eating the lilies, which supports Velez.

B.why: You restated background the passage already gives. Regional acidification would affect fenced and unfenced plots alike, so it can't explain why only the fenced plots recovered.

C.why: You overlooked what the passage reports: lily density rose in the fenced plots. A choice that contradicts the stated result can't be accepted as a finding.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Barreto's argument?
stimulus: A 1635 Dutch atlas and a 1592 Portuguese chart both place the mouth of the Ombeli River roughly forty kilometers north of where it lies today. Because the Dutch atlas was made later, historian Inês Barreto argues that its mapmakers did not survey that stretch of coast themselves. Instead, she says, they copied the coastline from the Portuguese chart and reproduced the chart's error.
choices: Sediment cores show that the Ombeli's mouth lay where both maps place it until a flood moved it in the 1700s.
The Dutch atlas also repeats a misspelled coastal place name that appears on the earlier Portuguese chart.
The Dutch atlas shows inland settlements along the Ombeli in far more detail than the Portuguese chart does.
The Dutch atlas shows the Ombeli's mouth at the place where the river actually meets the sea today.
explanation: Barreto's argument only works if the shared river mouth is an error. Two mapmakers working independently are unlikely to make the same mistake, but they could easily record the same correct position. If the river really did reach the sea at that spot in the 1600s, the match no longer suggests copying.

B.why: You picked the choice that supports Barreto. A shared misspelling is another copied error, which makes copying more likely, not less.

C.why: You missed the scope of the claim. Barreto is talking only about the coastline. The mapmakers could have copied the coast and still got their inland detail from other sources.

D.why: You overlooked the passage's starting fact. Both maps place the river mouth about forty kilometers north of where it is today, so the atlas can't show the modern location.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Marsh's hypothesis?
stimulus: In a museum's collection of nineteenth-century relief prints, blues made with plant-based indigo have faded far more than blues made with the synthetic pigment Prussian blue. Conservator Leah Marsh notes that many of the prints hung in the museum's galleries for decades, while others stayed in closed albums. She hypothesizes that the indigo faded because of light exposure, and that the fading occurred mainly in prints that were put on display.
choices: Indigo prints that hung in the galleries have faded much more than indigo prints that stayed in albums.
Prussian blue prints that hung in the galleries have faded slightly more than those that stayed in albums.
Indigo prints that stayed in closed albums have faded about as much as indigo prints that hung in the galleries.
Prussian blue prints in the collection have faded more, on average, than the indigo prints have.
explanation: Marsh's hypothesis is limited to light exposure and to the prints that were displayed. If it's true, indigo prints kept in the dark should have faded less. If the album prints faded just as much, light can't be what caused the fading.

A.why: You picked the choice that supports the hypothesis. More fading in displayed indigo prints is exactly what Marsh predicts.

B.why: You were drawn by the display-versus-album comparison but missed the pigment. Marsh's hypothesis is about indigo, so how Prussian blue behaves doesn't test it.

D.why: You reversed the passage's basic observation. The indigo blues faded far more than the Prussian blues, not the other way around.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Adeyemi's conclusion?
stimulus: When County A raised its minimum wage by 15 percent in 2021, many predicted that its restaurants would cut jobs. They did not: restaurant employment held steady over the next two years. Economist Ruth Adeyemi points out that higher pay tends to keep workers from quitting, and fewer departures mean fewer costly rounds of hiring and training. She concluded that these savings, by offsetting the larger wage bill, are what allowed restaurants to avoid cuts.
choices: The rate at which County A restaurant workers quit was no lower after the wage increase than before it.
County A restaurant workers were much less likely to quit their jobs after the wage increase than before it.
Most County A restaurant owners said in a survey that they had considered cutting staff after the increase.
Restaurant employment in County A fell sharply during the two years that followed the wage increase.
explanation: Adeyemi's explanation is a chain: higher pay leads to fewer quits, fewer quits lead to lower hiring and training costs, and those savings offset the wage bill. If quitting didn't decline, the middle link is gone. There would be no savings to explain why the restaurants kept their staff.

B.why: You picked the choice that supports the conclusion. Fewer quits is the first step in Adeyemi's chain, so this choice backs her explanation.

C.why: You treated a related detail as if it tested the claim. Owners can consider cuts without making them, so this tells you nothing about why they kept their staff.

D.why: You contradicted a fact the passage states: restaurant employment held steady. The question asks you to challenge the explanation for that fact, not to deny the fact itself.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Malhotra's claim?
stimulus: In 2022, the city of Harlow Falls installed protected bike lanes on six downtown avenues, removing one car lane from each. Within a year, weekday car counts on those six avenues had fallen by 18 percent. Some residents suggested that drivers had simply moved to nearby streets. City planner Dev Malhotra, however, claims that the lanes reduced car trips across the downtown district as a whole, not just on the avenues themselves.
choices: Weekday car counts across the downtown district as a whole fell after the bike lanes were installed.
The number of cyclists using the six avenues more than doubled within a year of the lanes opening.
Weekday car counts on the six avenues rose during the year after the bike lanes were installed.
Weekday car counts on streets parallel to the six avenues rose by about as many cars as the avenues lost.
explanation: Malhotra claims car traffic fell across the whole district. If the parallel streets gained about as many cars as the avenues lost, total traffic stayed roughly the same and drivers just moved. That is the residents' explanation, and it directly undercuts Malhotra.

A.why: You sided with the person whose claim you were asked to weaken. A district-wide drop is exactly what Malhotra predicts, so this choice supports him.

B.why: You picked a finding on the right topic but the wrong measure. More cyclists doesn't show whether car trips disappeared or just moved to other streets.

C.why: You contradicted the passage, which says car counts on the six avenues fell by 18 percent.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Holm's conclusion?
stimulus: Silk was never produced in medieval Norway, so historians long assumed that silk fragments found in Norwegian graves had arrived as finished cloth. Textile historian Sigrid Holm challenges that view for one fourteenth-century fragment. Its yellow color comes from a dye made from a lichen that grows only in Scandinavia. Holm concludes that the fragment was woven in Norway from imported raw silk.
choices: Lichen dye of the same kind has been found on wool threads woven at Norwegian sites of that period.
Several other silk fragments from Norwegian graves of the period contain no lichen dye at all.
Microscopic analysis shows that the lichen dye was applied to the cloth after it had already been woven.
The lichen used for the dye also grew widely in the regions where silk cloth was woven.
explanation: Holm's evidence is a local dye, but her conclusion is about local weaving. That step only works if the silk was dyed before it was woven. If the dye went onto the finished cloth, the cloth could have been woven abroad, imported, and then dyed in Norway, which fits the earlier historians' view.

A.why: You picked a choice that supports Holm. Evidence that Norwegians dyed thread with this lichen before weaving makes her account more believable.

B.why: You moved away from the one fragment Holm discusses. Other fragments being imported doesn't tell you where this one was woven.

D.why: This would weaken Holm if it were allowed, but the passage says the lichen grows only in Scandinavia. A choice can't contradict a fact the text states.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Reyes's conclusion?
stimulus: Larvae of the striped reef goby drift in open water for weeks before settling on a reef. To learn how they find one, marine biologist Tomás Reyes set up two identical tanks. In one, a speaker at the far end played recorded reef noise; the other tank was silent. Larvae in the first tank gathered near the speaker, while those in the silent tank spread out evenly. Reyes concluded that the larvae locate reefs mainly by sound rather than by smell.
choices: Larvae whose hearing had been impaired spread out evenly, even in a tank playing reef noise.
Given reef noise at one end of a tank and reef water at the other, most larvae gathered by the reef water.
Larvae in the silent tank clustered at the far end about as tightly as larvae in the speaker tank did.
Adult striped reef gobies that had already settled on a reef paid no attention to recorded reef noise.
explanation: Reyes's experiment only tested sound against silence, but his conclusion ranks sound above smell. If he's right, larvae offered both cues at once should go toward the noise. If most go toward the reef water instead, smell is the stronger cue, and his ranking is directly challenged.

A.why: You picked the choice that supports Reyes. If larvae that can't hear lose their sense of direction, that suggests sound is guiding them.

C.why: You contradicted the reported result. The passage says larvae in the silent tank spread out evenly.

D.why: You applied adult behavior to larvae. Reyes's claim is about how drifting larvae find a reef, and settled adults have no need to find one.
